lead: An aircraft material is never chosen on strength alone. The choice trades strength, stiffness, weight, fatigue life, temperature limit, corrosion and cost. A wing needs stiffness so it does not flex too much; a landing gear needs strength and toughness; an engine fitting needs heat resistance. Engineers compare materials using specific strength σ<sub>ult</sub>/ρ and specific stiffness E/ρ, where σ<sub>ult</sub> is ultimate tensile stress in Pa (N/m²), E is Young's modulus in Pa and ρ is density in kg/m³. These ratios let a light material compete with a strong heavy one. The same trade decides whether a part is aluminium, titanium, steel or carbon fibre.
prereq: You need: Honeycomb and sandwich structures for why light stiff faces matter.

blocks.text: Specific strength is ultimate tensile stress divided by density: σ<sub>ult</sub>/ρ. Specific stiffness is E/ρ. Units: (N/m²)/(kg/m³) = N·m/kg, also written J/kg or kN·m/kg. A high value means more load carried per kilogram of material. Use ultimate stress for strength comparisons. Use yield stress only when the design limits permanent deformation; mixing the two is a common error. The table gives typical room-temperature values; exact figures depend on the product form and temper. Composites are quoted along the fibre, because across the fibre they are much weaker.

blocks.where: σ<sub>ult</sub> is ultimate tensile stress in Pa (N/m²); ρ is density in kg/m³; the result is in N·m/kg.

blocks.text: One pattern in the table is worth remembering. Aluminium, titanium and steel all have E/ρ close to 25 MN·m/kg, so no metal beats another on specific stiffness; a stiffness-critical part gains nothing by changing metal. Only fibre composites break the pattern, with CFRP near 80 MN·m/kg along the fibre.

Aluminium is the default for wings and fuselage because it is light, stiff enough, cheap and easy to form. 2024 has copper and good fatigue resistance. It is used for tension skins but needs cladding or paint because it corrodes. 7075 uses zinc and has high strength. It is used in compression skins and fittings but has lower fatigue resistance and is sensitive to stress corrosion in the T6 temper. 6061 is weaker but welds well and resists corrosion, so it suits frames and secondary structure. Magnesium alloys are lighter than aluminium (ρ ≈ 1740 kg/m³) but have lower modulus (E ≈ 45 GPa), poor corrosion resistance and fire risk. Use is limited to small castings and older airframes. Titanium Ti-6Al-4V has density 4430 kg/m³, E ≈ 114 GPa and ultimate about 950 MPa. It keeps useful strength to roughly 300–400°C; special near-alpha titanium alloys reach about 500–550°C. It appears in engine parts, exhaust areas and highly loaded fittings. High-strength steels such as 300M have density 7850 kg/m³ and ultimate near 1950 MPa. They are used for landing gear and other compact, highly loaded parts where volume is tight and the weight penalty is accepted.

CFRP is carbon fibre in a polymer resin. The fibres carry the load; the resin holds the shape and passes shear between fibres. Along the fibre, CFRP has density about 1600 kg/m³, E of 70 to 150 GPa (70 for woven fabric, the higher values for one-direction tape) and tensile strength 1200 to 1800 MPa. It is very stiff and strong per kilogram, but its compressive strength is lower, impact damage can hide inside it, and the resin limits the temperature to about 120 to 180°C. GFRP uses glass fibre. It is cheaper and less stiff (E 20 to 40 GPa) and lets radar through, so it is used for radomes and fairings.

Fatigue. Aluminium alloys have no true endurance limit: their S-N curve keeps falling as cycles increase, so designers quote a fatigue strength at a chosen life (for example 10⁶ cycles) and design for damage tolerance. Steels do show a genuine endurance limit. 2024 is chosen for fatigue-critical tension skins because cracks grow slowly in it; 7075 is stronger but less forgiving. Composites have no single endurance limit either; they collect matrix cracks and delaminations, so design uses strain limits. The S-N curve itself is treated later, with fatigue and the endurance limit.

items: Corrosion: carbon fibre is cathodic to aluminium. A CFRP part bolted to aluminium makes the aluminium the anode and speeds up galvanic attack, so the joint is isolated with glass-fibre plies, sealant or coatings. 7075-T6 is prone to stress corrosion in the short-transverse direction; 2024 needs cladding or paint.
Temperature: aluminium alloys lose strength above about 120 to 150°C; titanium and steel go much higher.

Repair: aluminium panels are riveted or bolted; composites need bonded patches, a controlled cure and inspection. Joining is covered in Fabrication of structural components. Ply lay-up and laminate stiffness come later, with laminate theory; here only the choice of material matters.

examples.question: Compare the specific strength σ<sub>ult</sub>/ρ of three materials: 7075-T6 aluminium with σ<sub>ult</sub> = 570 MPa and ρ = 2810 kg/m³; Ti-6Al-4V with σ<sub>ult</sub> = 950 MPa and ρ = 4430 kg/m³; CFRP with σ<sub>ult</sub> = 1500 MPa and ρ = 1600 kg/m³. Give each answer in kN·m/kg and state which material wins on this ratio.
steps: Compare: CFRP is highest, then Ti-6Al-4V, then 7075-T6. CFRP still loses on compressive strength, temperature limit and repair.
examples.answer: CFRP has the highest specific strength, about 938 kN·m/kg, against 214 kN·m/kg for Ti-6Al-4V and 203 kN·m/kg for 7075-T6; it still loses on compression, temperature and repair.

traps: Quoting yield strength where ultimate strength is meant. Specific strength uses σ<sub>ult</sub> unless the design is explicitly limited by yield.
Comparing materials on strength alone. A strong heavy steel can lose to aluminium or CFRP once density, fatigue and temperature are included.
Forgetting the 10⁶ factor when converting MPa to Pa in σ/ρ. 570 MPa is 570 × 10⁶ Pa, not 570 Pa.
Treating CFRP as isotropic. Its fibre-direction strength is high, but transverse and compressive strengths are much lower.
Bolting carbon fibre directly to aluminium without isolation. Carbon is cathodic; the aluminium becomes the anode and corrodes fast.

quiz.q: Define specific strength and give its units when σ is in Pa and ρ is in kg/m³.
quiz.a: Specific strength is σ<sub>ult</sub>/ρ. Units are (N/m²)/(kg/m³) = N·m/kg, also written J/kg or kN·m/kg.

quiz.q: Why is 2024 aluminium often chosen for fatigue-critical fuselage skin instead of the stronger 7075?
quiz.a: 2024 has better fatigue resistance and damage tolerance. 7075 is stronger but less forgiving in fatigue and more sensitive to stress corrosion in some tempers. Fuselage skin is driven by fatigue and crack growth, not only static strength.

quiz.q: A material has σ<sub>ult</sub> = 400 MPa and ρ = 2000 kg/m³. Compute its specific strength in kN·m/kg.
CFRP wins the specific-strength comparison. Give two reasons it may still lose for a wing upper skin.
quiz.a: The upper skin is compression-critical, and CFRP compressive strength is lower than its tensile strength. Impact damage can be hidden and reduce compression strength. Resin temperature limits and repair difficulty also count against it. Aluminium may win after these knock-downs.

quiz.q: Name three aluminium alloys used in airframes and state one use for each.
quiz.a: 2024 for tension fuselage skin because of good fatigue resistance; 7075 for high-strength fittings and compression skins; 6061 for weldable frames and secondary structure.

quiz.q: What is the galvanic corrosion risk when CFRP is joined to aluminium, and how is it reduced?
quiz.a: Carbon fibre is cathodic to aluminium, so the aluminium becomes the anode and corrodes. Reduce it by isolating the joint with glass fibre plies, sealant, coatings or insulating fasteners.

quiz.q: Ti-6Al-4V has E = 114 GPa and ρ = 4430 kg/m³. Compute E/ρ in MN·m/kg.
Landing gear uses 300M steel with σ<sub>ult</sub> ≈ 1950 MPa despite a density of 7850 kg/m³. Explain why steel is still chosen.
quiz.a: The gear is strength- and stiffness-critical in a small volume, so it needs high absolute strength, toughness, impact resistance, fatigue performance and proven reliability; steel is also cheap and well characterised. Its specific strength (about 248 kN·m/kg) and specific stiffness (E/ρ ≈ 25 MN·m/kg) are competitive, so mass is not the deciding penalty — volume, toughness and cost are.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, designers use statistically based allowables from coupon and element tests, plus environmental knock-downs for moisture and temperature. Newer aircraft push composite share higher, so repair, inspection and lightning protection become material-selection issues, not just structural ones. Search next for specific strength, galvanic series, composite damage tolerance and material allowables.
